core: Working definition of business ethics: applying ethical principles — moral standards of right and wrong — to business decisions and conduct (CFI definition; OpenStax definition of ethics).
Ethical issue: a situation in which someone must choose between actions that may be ethical or unethical.
Why ethics matters: trust, reputation, and long-term survival; poor ethics is expensive and can end in bankruptcy and legal trouble.
Stakeholders: the individuals or groups to whom a business has a responsibility — owners/investors, employees, customers, and the community, each with one line.
Common ethical issues named generally: conflicts of interest, misleading claims, unfair treatment, environmental harm.
Three classic ethical lenses: consequences (utilitarian), duties (rights-based), virtues — each with one line.
Ethics versus law: legal is not always ethical; law is a floor, not a ceiling.
Honest framing: ethics is a practice, not a policy; it lives in everyday decisions.
supporting: Organizations encourage ethical conduct through employee education and leading by example (OpenStax).
Grey areas: practices that are not illegal but are still ethically questionable (CFI hotel-suite example used as an original-style illustration).
Recognizable categories of unethical activity: taking things that don't belong to you; saying things you know are not true; giving or allowing false impressions (OpenStax).
outOfScope: Management depth (planning, organizing, leading, controlling) — owned by management topic.
Business environment analysis (PEST etc.) — owned by business-environment topic.
Corporate social responsibility in depth (CSR strategy, reporting, philanthropy) — a practitioner topic.
Named-company scandal deep-dives — mentioned only as general phenomena, per source-map caution.
Political stances and advocacy — no positions taken.

claims.claim: Business ethics is the application of ethical principles to business decisions; ethics is a set of moral standards for judging whether something is right or wrong, and business ethics are the moral principles that act as guidelines for the way a business conducts itself and its transactions.
An ethical issue is a situation in which someone must choose between a set of actions that may be ethical or unethical.
Recognizable categories of unethical business activity include taking things that do not belong to you, saying things you know are not true, and giving or allowing false impressions.
Stakeholders are the individuals or groups to whom a business has a responsibility; the stakeholders of a business include its employees, its customers, the general public, and its investors.

A business's responsibility to employees includes a clean, safe working environment free from discrimination, and its responsibility to customers includes delivering what it promises and being honest and forthright in everyday interactions.

Poor business ethics can create a very negative image for a company, can be expensive for the firm and the executives involved, and can result in bankruptcy and legal trouble; organizations encourage ethical conduct by educating employees about ethical standards and by leading through example.
Ethics is not the same as following the law: a good system of law incorporates many ethical standards, but law can deviate from what is ethical and can be slow to address new problems.
Some business practices sit in grey areas: not illegal, yet ethically questionable — for example, hosting a supplier's negotiator in a top hotel suite in a way that edges toward bribery.

Three classic ethical lenses exist: the consequences (utilitarian) lens judges an action by the greatest balance of good over harm for everyone affected; the duties (rights) lens judges an action by whether it protects and respects the moral rights of those affected, and rights imply duties; the virtues lens asks whether an action is consistent with ideal character qualities such as honesty and integrity.

Good ethical decisions require a trained sensitivity to ethical issues and a practiced method for exploring them; ethics requires knowledge, skills, and habits and is practiced in everyday decisions rather than merely declared in policies.

positions: Markkula Center: ethics is not the same thing as following the law; a good system of law incorporates many ethical standards, but law can deviate from what is ethical and can be slow to cover new problems.
CFI: some practices are not illegal yet still ethically questionable (grey areas), e.g., hosting a supplier's negotiator in a top hotel suite.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the distinction simply: legal compliance is a floor, not a ceiling, and an action can be legal yet unethical.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many ethical lenses or frameworks should be taught?
positions: Markkula Center presents six lenses: rights, justice, utilitarian (consequences), common good, virtue, and care ethics.
The curriculum brief for this topic names three classic lenses: consequences, duties, and virtues.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the three classic lenses by name with one line each, and notes that other frameworks exist without cataloguing them.

positions: OpenStax: employees, customers, the general public, and investors.
Markkula's utilitarian lens names customers, employees, shareholders, the community, and the environment as affected parties.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the four core groups (owners, employees, customers, community) with one line each and folds the environment into the community line.

sourceRecords.title: A Framework for Ethical Decision Making
sourceRecords.provider: Markkula Center for Applied Ethics, Santa Clara University
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B (university ethics center). Verified live via HTTP fetch on 2026-08-21. Supports: ethics is not the same as feelings, religion, following the law, culturally accepted norms, or science; the rights (duties) lens — the ethical action best protects and respects the moral rights of those affected, and rights imply duties; the utilitarian (consequences) lens — the ethical action produces the greatest balance of good over harm for as many stakeholders as possible; the virtue lens — ethical actions are consistent with ideal virtues such as honesty, courage, compassion, and integrity, asking 'What kind of person will I become if I do this?'; and the claim that good ethical decisions require trained sensitivity and a practiced method.
